source_title: Experts flag ecological degradation, declining farming in Pindari region - The Times of India
source_excerpt: Nainital: Scientists and mountaineers have raised concerns over ecological degradation, declining traditional farming practices, increasing human-wildlife conflict and poor infrastructure in Pindari region of Uttarakhand.A team of scientist G S Rawat, and photographers Anup Sah and Aditya Chaudhary visited the upper Sarayu catchment in Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve in mid-Oct to assess its condition.Sah told TOI that farming in Khati village, the gateway to Pindari Glacier, was in decline as wild boars, monkeys, porcupines and langurs damaged crops, while leopards killed livestock. âMany villagers do not report their losses because the verification process takes too long and forest department offices are far from their homes,â he said. Also, fewer young people are taking up farming, Sah added.Wildlife has declined, forests have also deteriorated and medicinal plants have disappeared from parts of the region. Bhagichandra Singh Takuli, an 85-year-old resident of Jhuni village, recalled that the area was home to large numbers of musk deer, sambar, barking deer and Asiatic black bears about 50 years ago.Traditional beekeeping has also declined in Malla Danpur, once known for its honey and ghee. The scientists called for training in beekeeping, mushroom cultivation and cash-crop farming to help local people sustain their livelihoods.Rawat said poorly maintained tourist facilities were adding to the damage. âThe tourism department has built trails, rain shelters, igloo huts and viewpoints between Khati and Zero Point, but many have fallen into disrepair because of a lack of maintenance,â he said.He added, âPoorly planned and incomplete viewpoints and rain shelters in fragile alpine meadows have caused soil erosion, loss of vegetation and damage to the landscape.âExperts called for better maintenance of tourist facilities, limits on visitor numbers based on the areaâs capacity and greater involvement of local communities in conservation.In Jatoli village, a womenâs self-help group has banned the sale and consumption of alcohol and imposed fines on people who throw plastic wrappers and bottles along village paths. Experts said such community-led efforts could help protect the biosphere reserve if authorities encouraged and replicated them across the region.
